“Saudi air defences have been able to intercept some Houthi missile and drone attacks, but Saudi Arabia is so large that it’s simply impossible for them to consistently defend themselves,” said Thomas Juneau, a security analyst at the University of Ottawa.
Other analysts point out that even the vaunted Israeli air defence systems failed to stop a ballistic missile narrowly missing Ben Gurion international airport last year.

Reprisals against the Houthis and efforts to pre-emptively destroy the movement’s offensive capabilities are not easy either. The US bombardment in 2025 showed how hard it is to destroy the militia’s capabilities, which have been much enhanced over recent years, in part through Iranian advice and investment.

The Houthis say their actions were “guided by reciprocity” – suggesting they are responding to ongoing Saudi strikes on the territory they control in Yemen – but show no sign of stopping their attacks.
“Unless the Saudi enemy stops its aggression and interference in Yemen, worse is yet to come, God willing,” official statements carried by the Houthi-run al-Masirah television channel said.

It seems unlikely Saudi Arabia will halt its counterstrikes, and equally unlikely the kingdom will be able to find a way to block all incoming Houthi missiles, though it may improve its intelligence gathering and early warning to allow better defence of specific high-value targets.

Nor is there any imminent prospect of an end to the hostilities between Iran and the US that are a major factor in the surge of the recent violence in Yemen. And though the Houthis are more a coalition of different factions than a coherent single movement, for the moment they appear unified behind hardline and ideologically committed leaders.
Farea al-Muslimi, a specialist on Yemen and the Gulf at Chatham House in London, said the Houthis had been consistently underestimated over the years.

“They have really upped their game and believe they can get something now which will reposition them within the region. They are very confident at the moment and feeling empowered …. But though they think they can control this [escalation], that may well be an illusion,” he said.

articles.title: Former Irish Olympic swimming coach and child abuser George Gibney jailed for 15 years
articles.summary: Gibney, 78, has faced justice for abusing athletes in the 1970s and 80s after decades of effort to track and extradite him
body: More than half a century after he started sexually abusing children, and enjoyed prestige as Ireland’s Olympic swimming coach before fleeing to the United States, George Gibney has faced justice.
The 78-year-old was sentenced to 15 and a half years in prison at the central criminal court in Dublin on Monday for abusing four young female athletes in the 1970s and 1980s.
It was the culmination of a decades-long effort by victims, police, journalists and others to track down and extradite Gibney from the US.
He was convicted in July of 39 counts of indecent assault and one count of attempted rape after a closely watched trial that detailed harrowing abuse.

Judge Micheál P O’Higgin called Gibney a “manipulative predator” who had insinuated himself into the lives of children under his care. “It was predatory in nature and a gross breach of trust,” he said. “He used his coaching role to access and assault defenceless children under his care.”
The judge said Gibney had once enjoyed a stellar reputation and that the sentence reflected the gravity of his offending. “From these heights he has fallen, and his reputation now lies in tatters.”
The former coach, seated in a wheelchair, showed no emotion.
Speaking to reporters outside the court, Orla Poole said she had spent “decades in silence” because of his actions. “I thought I was the only one, that somehow, I deserved what he did to me.”

She said other survivors should know that they were not alone and could seek support. “The only guilt for what we went through lies with the convicted paedophile. When you are ready and able, unburden yourself by talking to someone from the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre, One In Four, a therapist, a trusted friend or even the gardaí.”

Evin Daly, a child welfare advocate who helped to find Gibney in Florida, said the sentence was vindication for Gibney’s victims. “The abuse shaped some of their lives. The guy had no conscience, in my opinion.”

Ireland had little international success in swimming in the 1980s but Gibney became a high-profile, respected figure for establishing the Trojan club in south Dublin and for coaching emerging talent at pools around the city. He was Ireland’s coach for the Olympic games in Los Angeles in 1984 and Seoul in 1988. Gibney urged his swimmers to “never give up” and to “hang in there”.

After allegations emerged that he preyed on children at pools, in his car and other locations, he was charged with 27 counts of indecency and carnal knowledge, but in 1993 the supreme court ruled that he could not face trial because of the time that had elapsed since the alleged offences, a decision that stunned his victims.
Free but infamous, Gibney moved to Scotland, then the US, where he obtained a visa and built a new life, living in Colorado, California and Florida and working mostly in low-level clerical jobs.
Several journalists continued to dig into Gibney’s crimes, including Justine McCarthy of the Irish Times who wrote a 2009 book, Deep Deception.
Related: Gary O’Toole: 'There are people like George Gibney in every sphere of society' | Donald McRae
Daly, a forensic sociologist who was then the chief executive of a child protection advocacy group called One Child International, helped the media to locate and keep tabs on Gibney.

“We provided data and resources,” said Daly, a Florida-based court consultant on child welfare cases. “At one point Gibney moved because his neighbours in the apartment complex got wind of the fact that he was an accused sex offender and they turned on him.”
In 2020 a 10-part podcast series, commissioned by the BBC and presented by Mark Horgan, titled Where is George Gibney? revived attention and scrutiny.

Four victims who were minors when they were abused made statements to Irish police between 2020 and 2022, leading to fresh charges, an extradition warrant and Gibney’s arrest and return to Ireland last year.
After the conviction in July four victims told the court of the impact of the abuse.
One said she retained “intensely personal and traumatic memories” and had harboured a “secret shame, hurt and bewilderment” for more than half a century. The abuse was a “frozen nightmare”, she said.

Another victim, who was nine at the time of the assaults, told Gibney in court that he had abused his position of trust and that her burden of shame, guilt and embarrassment was now his. Gibney had presided over “the destruction of a previously happy and healthy child” who was powerless to verbalise her torment, she said.

The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adult survivors on 0808 801 0331. In the US, call or text the Childhelp abuse hotline on 800-422-4453. In Australia, children, young adults, parents and teachers can contact the Kids Helpline on 1800 55 1800, or Bravehearts on 1800 272 831, and adult survivors can contact Blue Knot Foundation on 1300 657 380. Other sources of help can be found at Child Helplines International

articles.title: German minister quits after ‘indecent’ attacks intensify during bereavement
articles.summary: Fragile coalition suffers another blow as labour minister and co-leader of SPD Bärbel Bas leaves both posts
body: Germany’s labour minister and co-leader of the centre-left ⁠Social Democrats (SPD), Bärbel Bas, has quit both posts, citing the death of her stepdaughter and subsequent political attacks against her, in a stinging blow to the fragile coalition government.
“After my stepdaughter’s death, I realised that I need time to come to terms with my grief,” Bas said in a statement posted on Facebook, without giving further ⁠details.

Explaining her departure from frontline politics, Bas explicitly blamed public broadsides against her as she grappled with the family tragedy, “unfortunately also from among the ranks of the coalition partner [Friedrich Merz’s conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU)]”.
She said the attacks “continued to intensify during this difficult time for me personally”.

Some CDU lawmakers had criticised Bas’s absences during a crunch phase of an economic reform drive seen as crucial to the teetering government’s survival, although it was widely known she had experienced a death in her immediate family.

Bas’s co-leader at the SPD, Lars Klingbeil, who is also Merz’s vice-chancellor and finance minister, expressed regret at her departure and criticised the sniping against her while she was mourning as “indecent”.
Klingbeil cancelled a planned trip to India to deal with the fallout from Bas’s resignation, and complained about a degradation of the national political discourse.
“We are ​competitors, and we need ​a culture ‌of debate. ​But ​we also need a culture of mutual respect,” Klingbeil told reporters.

Merz, who has been fighting for his political survival after three disastrous state elections for his CDU last month, thanked Bas for “cooperation based on trust” in government and offered his condolences.
“As a father and grandfather, I can only imagine how deeply felt this loss is for you. I wish you and your family strength,” he wrote on X.

Alice Weidel, co-leader of the far-right Alternative für Deutschland, also gave Bas her sympathies but said her angry words towards the CDU demonstrated that Merz’s coalition government “is at its end”. She added: “We need a fresh start for Germany.”
The AfD, Germany’s biggest opposition party, is leading national opinion polls at about 30% after a strong showing in September’s regional elections, which also resulted in gains for the hard left.
Bas, who will remain an MP for Duisburg in the former Ruhr mining region, is a former president of the Bundestag lower house of parliament and one of the most experienced members of the SPD.
Her ministry oversees large parts of Germany’s costly social welfare system, which Merz has targeted for cuts.

While a representative of the party’s left wing, Bas was widely seen as a constructive team player able to bridge the kind of implacable policy disputes that have plagued Merz’s government since its inception in May 2025.
Her absence will now be keenly felt.

The coalition is deeply divided over plans to revive the sputtering economy, the EU’s largest, with Merz spearheading a pro-business savings drive and the SPD insisting on maintaining protections of workers’ rights and benefits.
The pension system is in particularly urgent need of reform as German society rapidly ages but plans to gradually lift the retirement age have met with angry resistance.

Approval ratings for Merz and his government have plunged over the course of the year, with voters fearing further deindustrialisation in the face of Chinese competition and steep rises in the cost of living.
Merz, a former corporate lawyer, is often perceived as haughty and out of touch, compounding his administration’s woes and giving rise to calls to replace him at the helm.
He has vowed to stay in office and fight for his policy agenda, saying it was the only way to beat back the “poison of authoritarianism” with extremists on the march.
The next general election is due in 2029 but five more state polls loom next year.
One of Merz’s cabinet ministers, Karin Prien, sounded the alarm last week, publicly calling for a change of course in the CDU away from Merz’s harsher stances and rhetoric.

“We bit our tongues for two or three years but that’s no longer an option,” the family affairs minister told Reuters ahead of a weekend party leadership meeting, referring to its centrist wing. “The ‘pure CDU’ approach (pursued by Merz) has failed.”
